2.text: of the village. He may have tea and tobacco, reindeer-tallow, or American

3.text: brandy. He is expected to give some of these to be added to the daily fare

4.text: of the house he stops in. Still usually he gives but very sparingly, often only

5.text: “just enough to smell,” as the Chukchee say. The same rule exists among

6.text: all the peoples of northeastern Asia that travel with dogs: in Kamchatka and

7.text: on the Anadyr, on the Lena, Kolyma, and Indighirka Rivers; on the shore

8.text: of the Okhotsk Sea, among natives as well, as among the Russian creoles.

9.text: Without such hospitality, journeying with dogs would be impossible, because

10.text: the little dried food one can carry on the sledge must be kept for halts in the

11.text: open country, and for other special occasions. Therefore people who live along

12.text: some well-visited route have to provide food, not so much for themselves as

13.text: for possible guests; and the amount required for the latter is more than that

14.text: required for the people themselves. Thus the inhabitants of the village

15.text: Mɪˊs˙qän — which lies on the route from Indian Point to the mouth of the

16.text: Anadyr, and, moreover, represents the last inhabited point before crossing

17.text: the long and lifeless tundra, — often have to feed some twenty complete dog-

18.text: teams, with more than two hundred animals. Mɪˊs˙qän has only three houses:

19.text: so this hospitality becomes a heavy burden. The same may be said of those

20.text: few Chukchee families who live on the Middle Anadyr, exactly halfway between

21.text: Markova and the mouth of the river. Each of these families slays every

22.text: summer about three hundred wild reindeer while they are crossing the river;

23.text: but the greater part of this large quantity of meat is consumed by the dogs

24.text: of Russian creoles passing to and fro for trading-purposes. Every time I asked

25.text: people in Mɪˊs˙qän or in Under-the-Cliffs, on the Middle Anadyr, as to the

26.text: game obtained during the preceding season, they would invariably answer,

27.text: “Enough for our wants, but too little for the passers-by.” Then they would

28.text: undertake some extra hunting in order to increase their supply; but no com-

29.text: plaint was ever uttered by any of them.

30.text: In other Maritime villages we were occasionally detained by a snow-storm

31.text: for several days. All fuel had been consumed. We fed on raw walrus-meat.

32.text: Still some fire was necessary to melt snow and to prepare the tea. In the

33.text: more southern villages, on the coast of the Pacific Ocean cooking is done

34.text: mostly, not with blubber, but with twigs from low bushes, small pieces of

35.text: driftwood, dried grass, etc. Then the house-master would take an axe and

36.text: break one of his sledges, or cut down one of the wooden house-supports at

37.text: the risk of its tumbling down on our heads. When we remember how scarce

38.text: wood is on the Arctic shore, and especially wood that is suitable for poles

39.text: and house-supports, we can appreciate the real value of such a sacrifice. The

40.text: few reindeer-breeders who live near the seacoast, scattered here and there

41.text: among the Maritime villages, have learned some of this hospitality; but those

42.text: living farther inland are very far from it.
